vignette:
The first time she tells me about leaving, her hands are folded in her lap, knuckles white. She speaks in a measured, almost librarian’s voice, as if she were cataloging a rare manuscript. She says it was a Tuesday in March, 1965. She was twenty-three, newly married, and she had just finished shelving books at the public library in San Salvador when her husband, Miguel, appeared at the door, breathless. He told her they had to leave. Right then. The soldiers had come to the university where he taught. They were looking for students. They were looking for anyone who had read the wrong poems.

She remembers running through the back streets, her skirt catching on a wire fence, the sound of boots on cobblestones behind them. A neighbor’s dog barked. She remembers the smell of diesel from a waiting truck, the rough canvas tarp that covered their heads, the way Miguel’s hand never let go of hers. They crossed the river at night, wading through cold water up to her ribs. She lost a shoe. She still dreams of that shoe, a black leather pump, sinking into mud.

Now she is seventy-eight, and she works behind the reference desk at a small branch library in a quiet Midwestern town. She has worked there for thirty years. She knows the Dewey Decimal System the way other people know the lines on their own palms. When a patron asks for help finding a book on Central American history, she feels her chest tighten. She points to the 972.8 section but does not walk them there. She stays behind the desk, straightening a stack of due-date cards, her fingers moving slowly, deliberately.

She has been married to Miguel for fifty-five years. He still teaches, now at a community college. He is the only one who knows the full story. But they do not talk about it. Not anymore. When the news plays images of refugees crossing borders, she gets up and walks to the kitchen. She fills the kettle, even if she has already made tea. She says she is not thirsty.

At night, she lies awake. She hears the river. She hears the boots. She feels the cold water on her skin. Sometimes she gets out of bed and goes to the living room. She pulls out the small cardboard box from the back of her closet—the one she has never shown her daughter, the one that holds her old identification card from El Salvador, a yellowed wedding photograph, and a single black lace glove. She does not open the box. She just places her hand on top of it, the way one might touch a wound that has not quite healed.

She avoids the news. She avoids crowded places. She avoids the sound of sirens, even though in this town sirens are rare. Last month, a car backfired in the library parking lot, and she dropped a stack of books. She said she was startled. She said it was nothing. But her hands shook for the rest of the afternoon, and she could not look at the librarian who came to help her.

She still works five days a week. It is her anchor. The library has order. The books are exactly where they are supposed to be. She knows every corner, every shelf. No one will come crashing through the door here. No one will ask her to choose between her country and her life. But sometimes, when a patron knocks on the reference desk to ask for help, she does not hear the question. She hears a truck engine, a river, a dog barking in the dark. She blinks, smiles, and asks them to repeat themselves. She always apologizes. She says she is getting older. She says her memory is not what it used to be. But the memory of that Tuesday morning in March — that memory is perfectly clear. It is as clear as the water she waded through, as sharp as the fence wire that tore her skirt. She cannot forget it. She can only shelve it, again and again, in a place she hopes no one will ever ask her to find.
